text: Yama, also known as Kāla, Dharmarāja, Pashi, and Kala, is the Hindu god of death and justice, responsible for dispensing law and punishing sinners in his abode, Naraka. He is often identified with Dharmadeva, the personification of Dharma, though they have distinct origins and myths. In Vedic tradition, Yama was the first mortal to die and discovered the path to the celestial abodes, becoming the ruler of the departed. He is described as the twin of the goddess Yami, the son of Surya (or Vivasvat) and Sanjna (or Saranyu), and is also the brother of Shraddhadeva Manu and the step-brother of Shani, with a son named Katila. Yama is one of the Lokapalas, the guardian of the south direction, and is depicted as a dark-complexioned man riding a buffalo, carrying a noose or mace to capture souls. He judges the souls of the dead and assigns them to the realm of the Pitris, Naraka, or rebirth on Earth. In the Rig Veda, Yama is the king of the dead, one of two kings humans see in heaven (the other being Varuna), and is associated with Agni, who is both his friend and priest. In the dialogue hymn RV 10.10, Yama and his twin sister Yamī debate whether to have sexual relations, with Yama ultimately refusing, though by RV 10.13.4, he is said to have chosen to have offspring. Yama is described in the Vedic texts as having a twin sister Yamī, residing in the highest heaven, and is stated to be unsurpassable and greater than Vivasvat. He has two four-eyed, broad-nosed, brindled, reddish-brown dogs, Sharvara and Shyama (or one dark), who track those about to die and guard the path to his realm. In the Taittirīya Aranyaka and Āpastamba Śrauta, Yama is said to have golden-eyed and iron-hoofed horses. In the Katha Upanishad, Yama teaches the Brahmin boy Nachiketa about the nature of being, knowledge, the Atman, and moksha. In the Mahabharata, Dharmadeva (identified with Yama) is the father of Yudhishthira, and appears in the Yaksha Prashna, where he tests Yudhishthira’s righteousness and reveals himself as his father, blessing him and restoring his brothers to life. In the Vana Parva, Yama arrives to take Satyavan’s soul after his death, but is impressed by Savitri’s devotion and allows her to bring him back to life. In the Tirtha-yatra Parva, it is stated that in the Satya Yuga, Krishna once performed the duties of Yama, leading to a time when no one died and the Earth sank for a hundred yojanas, prompting Varaha to lift it. In the Udyoga Parva, Yama’s wife is named Urmila or Dhumorna. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna states that among the dispensers of law, he is Yama, lord of death. In the Puranas, Yama is described as the lord of justice and is associated with Dharma; in the Agni and Linga Puranas, he is the son of Rajni and Surya. In the Srimad Bhagavatam, Yama is incarnated as a shudra named Vidura due to a curse by a sage, and during this time, Aryamā officiates as Yamarāja. Vidura, a devotee of Krishna, is revealed by Maitreya to be a former incarnation of Yamarāja, and Krishna states that sinners are torn apart by the vulture-like messengers of Yamarāja. A detailed account of a sinner’s punishment begins with their arrest by Yamadutas, who bind them with a rope, cover their subtle body, and carry them to Yamaloka, where they are bitten by dogs and remember their sins. In the sixth canto, Yama states that while he is a great controller of living entities, he is not supreme, as above him is the one supreme master, with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as partial manifestations. In the tenth canto, Krishna and Balarama travel to Yama’s abode, Saṁyamanī, where Yamarāja, upon hearing the conchshell, comes to bring back the dead son of Sandipani Muni. In the Brahma Purana, Yama is described as riding on a terrible buffalo, holding a sceptre, with a yellow body, unparalleled in strength, brilliance, and power, and wearing garlands. In the Garuda Purana, Yama’s realm and punishments are detailed, with his wife named Syamala. In the Matsya and Vishnu Puranas, Yama is mentioned extensively, including in battles against the asuras.

In the Brahma Purana, Yama is depicted as the lord of justice and is associated with Dharma; he rides on a terrible buffalo, holds a sceptre (rod of chastisement), has a yellow body, is unmatched in brilliance, strength, and power to demand obedience, possesses well-developed limbs, and wears garlands—described in Chapter 30.9–12 of the Brahma Purana. The Garuda Purana provides extensive details about Yama and his realm where sinners are punished, specifying that his wife is named Syamala. In the Matsya Purana, Yama is mentioned extensively in relation to his battles against the asuras. According to the Vishnu Purana, Yama is the son of the sun-god Surya (Vivasvan in the Vedas) and Sandhya (Saranya in the Vedas), daughter of Vishvakarma (Tvastar in the Vedas), who emerged from Vishvakarma’s navel; during a conversation with his servant, Yama states he is subordinate to Vishnu. Chapter 8 of Book 1 of the Vishnu Purana also describes Dhumorna (also known as Urmila) as Yama’s consort. Varying accounts across Hindu texts mention different consorts and children: the Mahābhārata, Vishnu Purana, and Vishnudharmottara identify Dhumorna (Urmila) as Yama’s consort; the Garuda Purana names Syamala as his wife; some texts list three consorts—Hema-mala, Sushila, and Vijaya; and when identified with Dharmadeva, he is said to have married 10 or 13 daughters of the god Daksha. The Brahma Purana names Sunita as Yama’s eldest daughter, who is the mother of king Vena, and Sobhavati, the wife of Chitragupta, is sometimes considered Yama’s daughter. In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, is blessed by Dharma to his mother Kunti. The Yama Dharmaraja Temple is located in Thiruchitrambalam, Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, India, and is dedicated to Yama. Yama is mentioned in the Pāli Canon of Theravada Buddhism and later entered Buddhist mythology in East Asia, Southeast Asia, and Sri Lanka as a Dharmapala; he is also recognized in Sikhism. In addition to scriptural depictions, Yama has been portrayed in movie and television adaptations, including in the series "The Star-Touched Queen" and "A Crown of Wishes" by Roshani Chokshi, and has also been featured in road safety campaigns in India, particularly to warn against the dangers of riding motorcycles without helmets.
